subject: Critical Thinking
title: Hasty Generalization: One Example Isn't a Pattern
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Hasty Generalization: One Example Isn't a Pattern.

hook.text: 'I met a rude person from that country. People from there must be rude.' One data point. 7 billion people. Sure.

buildup.text: Hasty generalization: drawing a broad conclusion from a sample that's too small or unrepresentative.

twist.text: Media amplifies this: one plane crash creates 'flying is dangerous.' One tech CEO success creates 'drop out of college.'

climax.text: Good reasoning asks: How large is the sample? Is it representative? Are there counterexamples?

punchline.text: Anecdotes are not data. No matter how vivid.

quiz.question: What makes a hasty generalization fallacious?
options: Drawing conclusions too quickly in time
Drawing broad conclusions from a sample that's too small or unrepresentative

details.summary: A hasty generalization draws a broad conclusion from too few examples. Meeting one rude person from a city and concluding everyone there is rude is classic hasty generalization.
details.whyItMatters: Stereotypes, prejudices, and many erroneous beliefs form through hasty generalization. A single experience does not make a pattern.
takeaways: Conclusions need sufficient and representative evidence
Stereotypes are often hasty generalizations made permanent

faq.question: How many examples do you need before a generalization is justified?
faq.answer: There is no fixed number. The sample must be large enough and representative enough to support the conclusion's scope. A generalization about all birds requires observations across many species and environments.

faq.question: Why are first impressions so prone to hasty generalization?
faq.answer: First impressions are based on a single encounter that may be atypical. Combined with primacy bias and the halo effect, one experience can crystallize into a permanent judgment that resists correction from later evidence.
